newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Aleman to take power as Nicaragua's leftists rage.
newsitem.headline: Aleman to take power as Nicaragua's leftists rage.

text.p: Right-winger Arnoldo Aleman, who becomes Nicaragua's president on Friday, faces an immediate political crisis from left-wing Sandinistas, and rumblings of violence in the countryside.

Aleman, a 50-year-old lawyer and coffee farmer, was scheduled to don the presidential sash around midday (1800 GMT) in Managua's Rigoberto Lopez Perez Stadium before 22,000 spectators, seven Latin American presidents and delegations from 61 nations.

Aleman replaces outgoing President Violeta Chamorro, 67, a gray-haired, motherly figure who has lauded the transfer of power as the consolidation of Nicaragua's fledgling democracy, born in 1990 to quench the flames of civil war.

In a chilling reminder of that violent past, an unknown armed group on Thursday ambushed an army patrol, leaving six Nicaraguans soldiers -- including a major and two captains -- dead and four injured in the central province of Matagalpa, a police spokesman said.

Aleman, the former mayor of the capital Managua, takes over a country wracked by poverty and a bitter polarisation between its two main political forces, the left-wing Sandinista Front and Aleman's right-wing Liberal Alliance coalition.

This hostility boiled over late on Thursday, as the Sandinista bench stormed out of the new National Assembly's inaugural session, angered by a Supreme Electoral Council ruling they said undermined the rule of law in Nicaragua.

The Sandinistas' reaction came two days after the Supreme Court struck down 80 Sandinista-sponsored laws in a ruling former Sandinsta President Daniel Ortega described as a "coup d'etat" and "a death sentence for the rule of law."

"We are not going to be complices in a process that is affecting the legitimacy, the legality, the constitutional order and the rule of law," said Ortega, the head of the Sandinista bench, before abandoning the building.
With the 36 Sandinista legislators absent from the 93-seat parliament, the remaining legislators elected a Liberal-dominated leadership for the National Assembly.

With the Liberals now controlling the government, parliament and judiciary, Victor Hugo Tinoco, second to Ortega in the Sandinista delegation, warned that they would have to take their protests to the streets.

"They are forcing the people to resolve their problems in the streets. Nicaragua is nearing a dictatorship. It is nearing a response from the people to the methods of a dictatorship," he told reporters.

Aware that Nicaragua's political stability and hopes for a successful term in office partly ride on his reaching a truce with the still-powerful Sandinistas, Aleman extended an olive branch to Ortega.

"Two, three days after the inauguration, I'm going to go to Daniel Ortega's house and invite him and the Sandinista Front to join us, and all the active forces, business, the workers, to form a national concertation to move this country forward," Aleman said in an interview with CBS Telenoticias.
Analysts have warned that any political instability will scare away desperately needed foreign investment.
The Sandinistas, who governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990, have a history of boisterous street protests and used their muscle to frustrate the Chamorro government in its early years.

Aleman takes over the second-poorest country in Latin America, still recovering from its economic collapse in the 1980s. Nicaragua's economy grew by 5.5 percent in 1996, and was expected to continue growing in 1997.
Police said 2,300 officers were assigned to protect the event, guarding the stadium, key plazas and hotels.
